Hirschsprung's disease can be congenital or acquired. In neonates, it is usually diagnosed through the "bible" sign (upon digital rectal examination, the rectal ampulla is dilated and forms a smooth, blind ending, within two feet of the anorectal ring) or failure to pass meconium within 48 hours of birth.  Presentation can also include:[distal intraluminal exam] - a narrow, smooth unit of bowel, distal to the transition zone, which is dilated and forms a rectal-like dilation. [apernas renales] - bilateral megacalyces (enlarged renal pelvis) on ultrasound, due to the high position of the aganglionic segment. [pneumocele] - enterocolitis (inflammation of bowel lining) with gas in the wall of the bowel.  The condition is caused by an aganglionic segment of bowel, with a lack of motor neurones, resulting in an inability of the smooth muscle to relax, thus causing bowel obstruction.  Congenital Hirschsprung's disease is caused by failure of neural crest cells to migrate fully into the developing gut, whereas acquired is due to lymphedrainage disorders, malignancy, sepsis, etc.  Other anomalies:associated deafness (otaic), mile's eye (arythmopsia), duodenal atresia, imperforate anus, etc.

Hyperthyroidism is commonly caused by Grave's disease (70%), toxic multinodular goitre (25%) and thyroid cancer (5%). Patients with Grave's disease are thought to have an increased sensitivity to T4 from the body's most potent pyrimidine organ, the thyroid gland.  Treatment options for hyperthyroidism include antithyroid drugs, radioactive iodine, surgery and, rarely, glucocorticoid and insulin therapy in crisis.  Carbimazole is an antithyroid drug that inhibits iodine uptake from the circulation into the thyroid gland, thus reducing T4 and T3 synthesis.  Radioactive iodine therapy works by ablating the thyroid gland - iodine is concentrated in the gland and RAI makes beta rays to which the thyroid is sensitive, leading to destruction and usually requiring a peratenary L-thyroid replacement.  Glucocorticoids are thought to have a suppressive effect on T4 and T3 from the peripheral metabolisation of thyroglobulin, and insulin may help to transport the thyroid hormones from the plasma into the intracellular compartment where they exert their effects.  Levothyroxine and T3 are synthetic thyroid hormones and are not used in hyperthyroidism (though they are used in hypothyroidism).
